definition: An approach often described as 'learning to learn,' where a model is trained across many tasks so that it can adapt quickly to new, related tasks with minimal additional data.
details: Meta-learning is closely related to few-shot learning, and has influenced how researchers think about the in-context learning capabilities that emerge in large language models.

explainer.lead: Meta-learning, often called learning to learn, trains a model across many tasks so it can adapt quickly to new, related tasks with minimal additional data. It matters because that fast adaptation is what makes few-shot performance possible.

tiers.eli5: It is like practising many different sports so that a brand-new game is easy to pick up after a few tries. You are training the skill of learning quickly, not one specific game.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers train across many tasks so that a small amount of data from a new task yields fast adaptation. The pitfall is that the training task distribution must resemble the target task, or the quick adaptation does not carry over.
tiers.paperLevel: Training a model over a distribution of tasks so it can adapt to new, related tasks with minimal additional data; it is closely related to few-shot learning. Its limits come from how well the training task distribution matches the tasks encountered later.

explainer.example: A model trained on many classification tasks adapts to a new class from only a handful of labelled examples.
